paper_sections.title: Conscious and unconscious brain responses to food and cocaine cues
Main effect of time of day

description.value: The study examined brain responses to food, cocaine, and neutral visual cues presented subliminally or supraliminally, and tested whether cue reactivity differed between morning and evening sessions in healthy cocaine-naive volunteers.

design.value: Sixteen healthy volunteers underwent three fMRI sessions with cue presentation times of 33, 750, and 3000 ms, each repeated on two separate days once in the morning and once in the evening in randomized order. The study used an event-related food cue reactivity task with food, cocaine-related, and neutral images.

task_description.value: A total of 40 appetitive food, 40 cocaine-related and 40 neutral images were presented in a randomized order in an event-related design. Three sessions used different cue presentation times: 33 ms, 750 ms and 3000 ms. Each task consisted of 3 runs showing 40 cues that included all 3 categories of cues. The 33 ms cues were followed by a 467 ms neutral mask; there was no backward masking for the 750 ms or 3000 ms tasks. Each participant performed the three sessions twice on two separate days, once between 9 and 11 AM and once between 5 and 7 PM, in randomized order.

instructions.value: To ensure that participants were paying attention they were instructed to press a button if they saw an animal.

stimuli.value: Food pictures included appetitive high and low calorie foods, both savory and sweet, both breakfast and dinner items. Cocaine pictures included bags of cocaine, lines of cocaine on a table, cocaine in spoons, cocaine pipes, and people smoking cocaine, with faces cut off. Neutral pictures included neutral items from the International Affective Picture System and from in-house picture libraries. Picture groups were matched for luminance.

description.value: A standard echo planar imaging (EPI) sequence was used with sequential interleaved acquisition, 64×64 pixels in-plane resolution, 36 slices, slice thickness 4 mm, voxel dimensions 3×3×4 mm3, and field of view 192×192 mm2. Stimuli were presented on a black background under dimmed room lighting using a liquid-crystal display screen (BOLDscreen 32, Cambridge Research Systems; UK).

instrument.value: 3 T Magnetom Prisma scanner (Siemens Medical Solutions USA, Inc., Malvern, PA)

description.value: T1 structural images were used for co-registration of the functional data.

Functional data analysis was performed with SPM8. During preprocessing, scans were slice-time corrected, spatially realigned, co-registered to the T1 structural images and normalized to the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) template. Smoothing was performed with a 6 mm full-width at half-maximum Gaussian kernel. Two participants had excessive head motion during their MRI scans (>2 mm), resulting in n=14 participants for further fMRI analyses.

model_settings.value: Valence, arousal and wanting ratings were modeled with two factors: cue type (food, cocaine, neutral) and time of day (AM, PM). Post-hoc t-tests tested whether cues were rated differently than 0.

For every participant and for each session (33, 750 or 3000 ms), three fMRI regressors—food, cocaine, and neutral events—were created and convolved with the hemodynamic response function with default temporal filtering of 128 s. Six realignment parameters were included as regressors of no interest. Single-subject contrasts were food>neutral, food>cocaine, and cocaine>neutral.

The second-level design included first-level contrast images with presentation time (33, 750 and 3000 ms) and time of day (AM and PM) as within-subject factors. Whole-brain analyses tested main effects of food>neutral, food>cocaine, and cocaine>neutral, subliminal versus supraliminal presentation times, and morning versus evening effects. The combined threshold was p<0.005 uncorrected at the voxel level with family-wise error corrected pFWE<0.05 at the cluster level and minimum cluster size k>100; coordinates were reported in MNI space.
